reason: A careful reader coming to 'I seal up these records' from Isaiah 8:16 ('bind up the testimony, seal the law among my disciples') or Daniel 12:4 ('shut up the words, and seal the book, even to the time of the end') will feel the pull, and the Book of Mormon itself invites it: 2 Nephi 27 builds a whole prophecy out of Isaiah 29:11's sealed book. But the verbal contact at 10:2 is the single common verb 'seal', which occurs in twenty-five KJV verses and which the Book of Mormon uses as its own technical term for closing a record (2 Nephi 30:17, Ether 3:22, 4:5, 5:1). Nothing else of Daniel 12 or Isaiah 8 is present — no shutting, no time of the end, no disciples, no testimony bound. The eschatological sealed book is a real and important background to the plates, and it is adjudicated where the wording actually is, in 2 Nephi 27.

The chapter's top-ranked machine candidate at the chapter's most famous verse, on a five-word run, and it is the New Testament's standing prayer formula. 'In the name of' plus a christological title stands at Ephesians 5:20, Colossians 3:17, John 14:13-14, 16:23-24 and dozens of other places; Moroni 10:4's 'ask God, the Eternal Father, in the name of Christ' is that formula and no particular verse of it. The link at this verse is to James 1:5-6 and rests on the sequence of conditions, not on this phrase.

Scored 2.00, the highest in its verse, on a five-word run that is two prepositional phrases joined. Titus 1:1 has 'according to the faith of God's elect' as part of an apostolic salutation; Moroni 10:7 has 'according to the faith of the children of men' as a statement about the condition on which God's power operates — a doctrine the Book of Mormon states in these words repeatedly (Ether 12:12, 'if there be no faith among the children of men, God can do no miracle among them'). The construction is the book's own and its recurrence inside the corpus, not a borrowing from a salutation. 2 Corinthians 13:4's 'by the power of God', proposed at the same verse, is covered by the same reasoning: the phrase occurs in three KJV verses, none of which supplies anything else here, and it is Moroni's refrain through 10:5-10:7.

A genuine six-word run and the second-ranked candidate in a verse whose real source, 1 Corinthians 12:4-7, is not in doubt. The senses are opposed: Psalm 25:19 is 'Consider mine enemies; for they are many; and they hate me with cruel hatred', a complaint that the many are hostile, and Moroni 10:8 is 'ye deny not the gifts of God, for they are many', a reassurance that the many are gifts. The clause is a bare quantifier with a causal conjunction and it attaches to whatever noun precedes it. Romans 15:14 ('my brethren, that ye') and 1 Corinthians 2:14 ('of the Spirit of God: for they are'), proposed at the same verse, are covered here too — both are connective overlaps inside a verse already reproducing 1 Corinthians 12 verbatim.

Five words of pure back-reference. 'The place of which I have spoken unto thee' in Exodus 32:34 and 'all these gifts of which I have spoken' in Moroni 10:19 share a relative clause that any writer resuming an earlier topic will produce; the KJV has close variants at Genesis 24:7, Numbers 10:29 and elsewhere. The verse's actual sources, Hebrews 13:8 and 1 Corinthians 13:8-10, are adjudicated as links.

The five-word run is 'kingdom of God neither', and 'the kingdom of God' alone occurs in some sixty KJV verses. What makes the candidate tempting is that Paul's sentence, like Moroni's, states an exclusion from the kingdom — but Paul's excluded party is 'flesh and blood', a statement about the resurrection body, and Moroni's is the person without charity, a statement about a moral condition. The 'neither' that completes the run belongs in Paul to a second clause about corruption inheriting incorruption and in Moroni to the second and third terms of his own faith-hope-charity chain. The chain's source, 1 Corinthians 13:13, is adjudicated one verse earlier at 10:20.

sharedText: If ye have faith, ye can do all things
reason: The verse presents itself as a quotation — 'And Christ truly said unto our fathers, If ye have faith, ye can do all things which is expedient unto me' — and the reader's first instinct is to look for the saying in the Gospels: Mark 9:23 ('all things are possible to him that believeth'), Matthew 17:20 ('nothing shall be impossible unto you'), or Philippians 4:13 ('I can do all things through Christ'). None of them is the source. The saying quoted here is the Book of Mormon's own, at Moroni 7:33: 'And Christ hath said, If ye will have faith in me, ye shall have power to do whatsoever thing is expedient in me.' Moroni is quoting his own earlier chapter, which is itself quoting a dominical saying the Book of Mormon supplies and no Bible contains. The Gospel parallels are the background of the idea and not the source of the words, and this row records where the borrowing is actually adjudicated.

The four-word run is real and the source is right, but the verse where the argument is made is 10:19, where the same phrase is used to deny what Paul's chapter asserts — 'all these gifts … never will be done away'. Here at 10:24 the phrase recurs inside the hypothetical Moroni has already rejected ('if the day cometh that the power and gifts of God shall be done away among you'). Cataloguing it twice would double-count one borrowing. See the link at Moroni 10:19. Isaiah 26:15 and Malachi 4:1, proposed at this verse on 'all the ends of the earth' and 'the day cometh that', are formulaic: the first is the Book of Mormon's standing address to its readership (2 Nephi 33:10, 3 Nephi 27:20, Mormon 3:17) and the second is the KJV's standard prophetic opener.

A five-word run and the top candidate in its verse, and it very nearly is a composite source rather than an exclusion. But the overlap decomposes: 'no, not one' belongs to the clause Moroni is quoting from Psalm 14:3 / Psalm 53:3 / Romans 3:12, where it is fixed, and 'among you' is required by Moroni's second-person address ('there shall be none that doeth good among you'), which he has been sustaining since 10:24. Paul's sentence at 1 Corinthians 6:5 is a sarcasm about the Corinthians' inability to produce an arbitrator — 'is it so, that there is not a wise man among you? no, not one that shall be able to judge between his brethren?' — and it shares with Moroni neither the subject (a wise man, not a good man), the predicate (judging a dispute, not doing good), nor the argument. The link is filed at 10:25 with the three verses that carry the whole clause.

Five words of connective tissue. 'Ye shall know that' introduces a coming certainty in the KJV some forty times, from Exodus 6:7 onward, and Moroni's 'the time speedily cometh that ye shall know that I lie not' is that construction with the Book of Mormon's own idiom on either side of it. Paul's verse — 'I trust that ye shall know that we are not reprobates' — happens to share the frame and a defensive posture, but nothing beyond the frame. The verse's real source, Isaiah 29:4 by way of Nephi's farewell at 2 Nephi 33:13, is adjudicated as a link.

Hardy's apparatus cross-references Isaiah 29:4 at this verse. The verbal contact with Isaiah 29:4 — 'like as one crying from the dead? yea, even as one speaking out of the dust' — is in the preceding verse, 10:27, and the link is filed there with the Book of Mormon's own earlier renderings of the same Isaiah verse (2 Nephi 26:16, 2 Nephi 33:13). Moroni 10:28 itself says the words 'shall proceed forth out of the mouth of the everlasting God' and 'hiss forth from generation to generation', which are a different borrowing (Matthew 4:4, adjudicated here) and a Book of Mormon idiom for the going-out of the record (2 Nephi 29:3, 'because my words shall hiss forth'). Isaiah 5:26's 'he will hiss unto them from the end of the earth' is the Isaian background of that idiom, but 'hiss' occurs in twelve KJV verses, nine of them derisive rather than summoning, and the wording will not carry a link at this verse. This is a §6a move: our reading puts Hardy's reference one verse earlier, where the words are.

A four-word run against a verse whose Isaian sources are not in question. Ezekiel 24:17 is the prohibition of mourning for Ezekiel's wife — 'bind the tire of thine head upon thee, and put on thy shoes upon thy feet' — and the shared words are an imperative verb plus a possessive. Moroni 10:31 has 'put on thy beautiful garments', which is a King James singleton from Isaiah 52:1 and is adjudicated as such.

Worth a row only because of the variant. The 1830 reads 'ye can in no wise deny the power of God' at 10:32 and 'ye can in no wise be saved' at 10:21; the 1920 edition prints 'nowise' in both places, closing up a two-word King James phrase into a single word and, unusually for this book, moving the text away from KJV orthography rather than toward it (contrast 10:16, where 1920's 'divers' restores the KJV spelling against 1830's 'diverse'). The phrase itself occurs in eleven KJV verses across both testaments, several of them in Luke and Matthew's absolute constructions, and it identifies no source. The verse's real borrowings are Titus 2:12, 2 Corinthians 12:9 and Colossians 1:28, all adjudicated as links.

'I am brought forth triumphant through the air' invites Paul's 'thanks be unto God, which always causeth us to triumph in Christ' at the end of a book that has just been quoting Paul continuously, and a reader might well accept it. The contact is one word in a different part of speech: Paul's is a verb in a metaphor of a Roman triumphal procession, Moroni's an adjective describing a resurrected body in motion. The KJV has 'triumph' in ten verses and none of them supplies the rest of Moroni's sentence. What that sentence does borrow — the resurrection, the air, and the meeting — is adjudicated at 10:34 as an echo of 1 Thessalonians 4:16-17.
